claim: The eukaryotic genome is divided into multiple chromosomes and encapsulated in a single nucleus.
source: A universal and unquestioned characteristic of eukaryotic cells is that the genome is divided into multiple chromosomes and encapsulated in a single nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of eukaryotic cells in the abstract.

claim: The underlying mechanism to ensure genome encapsulation in a single nucleus is unknown.
source: However, the underlying mechanism to ensure such a configuration is unknown.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Pericentromeric satellite DNA is a critical constituent of the chromosome that allows packaging of all chromosomes into a single nucleus.
source: Here, we provide evidence that pericentromeric satellite DNA, which is often regarded as junk, is a critical constituent of the chromosome, allowing the packaging of all chromosomes into a single nucleus.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study presented in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster D1 and mouse HMGA1 are multi-AT-hook satellite DNA-binding proteins.
source: We show that the multi-AT-hook satellite DNA-binding proteins, Drosophila melanogaster D1 and mouse HMGA1, play an evolutionarily conserved role in bundling pericentromeric satellite DNA from heterologous chromosomes into 'chromocenters', a cytological association of pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: D1 and HMGA1 play an evolutionarily conserved role in bundling pericentromeric satellite DNA from heterologous chromosomes into chromocenters.
source: We show that the multi-AT-hook satellite DNA-binding proteins, Drosophila melanogaster D1 and mouse HMGA1, play an evolutionarily conserved role in bundling pericentromeric satellite DNA from heterologous chromosomes into 'chromocenters', a cytological association of pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing similar phenotypes in both Drosophila and mouse systems.

claim: Defective chromocenter formation leads to micronuclei formation due to budding from the interphase nucleus.
source: Defective chromocenter formation leads to micronuclei formation due to budding from the interphase nucleus, DNA damage and cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by live imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: Defective chromocenter formation leads to DNA damage.
source: Defective chromocenter formation leads to micronuclei formation due to budding from the interphase nucleus, DNA damage and cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by γ-H2Av/γ-H2Ax staining data in Figure 3.

claim: Defective chromocenter formation leads to cell death.
source: Defective chromocenter formation leads to micronuclei formation due to budding from the interphase nucleus, DNA damage and cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by testis degeneration data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chromocenter and satellite DNA serve a fundamental role in encapsulating the full complement of the genome within a single nucleus.
source: We propose that chromocenter and satellite DNA serve a fundamental role in encapsulating the full complement of the genome within a single nucleus, the universal characteristic of eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Satellite DNA is AT-rich, non-coding, repetitive DNA that is abundant in centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin.
source: Satellite DNA is AT-rich, non-coding, repetitive DNA that is abundant in centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The role of pericentromeric satellite DNA remains obscure.
source: Unlike the satellite DNAs that comprise the vast majority of natural centromeres (Willard, 1990; Sun et al., 1997, 2003), the role of pericentromeric satellite DNA remains obscure
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction, with citations to prior work on centromeric satellite DNA.

claim: Function for a few satellite DNA repeats has been implied in certain cellular processes such as meiotic segregation of achiasmatic chromosomes, X chromosome dosage compensation and formation of lampbrush-like loops on the Y chromosome during male meiosis.
source: although function for a few satellite DNA repeats has been implied in certain cellular processes such as meiotic segregation of achiasmatic chromosomes, X chromosome dosage compensation and formation of lampbrush-like loops on the Y chromosome during male meiosis (Yunis and Yasmineh, 1971; Bonaccorsi et al., 1990; Dernburg et al., 1996; Menon et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies that have implicated satellite DNA in specific functions.

claim: A unifying theme for pericentromeric satellite DNA function remains elusive.
source: although function for a few satellite DNA repeats has been implied in certain cellular processes such as meiotic segregation of achiasmatic chromosomes, X chromosome dosage compensation and formation of lampbrush-like loops on the Y chromosome during male meiosis (Yunis and Yasmineh, 1971; Bonaccorsi et al., 1990; Dernburg et al., 1996; Menon et al., 2014), a unifying theme for pericentromeric satellite DNA function remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Highly divergent satellite DNA sequences even among closely related species has led to the idea that satellite DNA does not serve a conserved function and is mostly a selfish element or junk.
source: Moreover, highly divergent satellite DNA sequences even among closely related species has led to the idea that satellite DNA does not serve a conserved function and is mostly a selfish element or junk (Doolittle and Sapienza, 1980; Walker, 1971).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature proposing satellite DNA as junk or selfish elements.

claim: Pericentromeric satellite DNA repeats are proposed to be sources of genomic instability.
source: Pericentromeric satellite DNA repeats are proposed to be sources of genomic instability, as their misexpression is associated with the formation of genotoxic R-loops and DNA damage (Zhu et al., 2011; Zeller et al., 2016; Zeller and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies linking satellite DNA misexpression to genomic instability.

claim: Misexpression of pericentromeric satellite DNA is associated with the formation of genotoxic R-loops and DNA damage.
source: Pericentromeric satellite DNA repeats are proposed to be sources of genomic instability, as their misexpression is associated with the formation of genotoxic R-loops and DNA damage (Zhu et al., 2011; Zeller et al., 2016; Zeller and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Most studies on pericentromeric heterochromatin have focused on the mechanisms to repress satellite DNA transcription.
source: Most studies on pericentromeric heterochromatin have focused on the mechanisms to repress satellite DNA transcription, and accordingly, a clear rationale for the existence of most pericentromeric satellite DNA is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the research focus in the field.

claim: A clear rationale for the existence of most pericentromeric satellite DNA is still lacking.
source: Most studies on pericentromeric heterochromatin have focused on the mechanisms to repress satellite DNA transcription, and accordingly, a clear rationale for the existence of most pericentromeric satellite DNA is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Pericentromeric satellite DNA from multiple chromosomes is clustered into chromocenters in interphase nuclei in diverse eukaryotes including Drosophila, mouse and plants.
source: Cytologically, it is well documented that pericentromeric satellite DNA from multiple chromosomes is clustered into chromocenters in interphase nuclei in diverse eukaryotes including Drosophila, mouse and plants (Figure 1A) (Jones, 1970; Pardue and Gall, 1970; Gall et al., 1971; Fransz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior cytological studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Multiple factors such as epigenetic modifications and transcription of repetitive DNA from pericentromeric DNA sequences are known to be required for chromocenter formation.
source: While multiple factors such as epigenetic modifications and transcription of repetitive DNA from pericentromeric DNA sequences are known to be required for chromocenter formation (Peters et al., 2001; Probst et al., 2010; Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012; Pinheiro et al., 2012; Hahn et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies on chromocenter formation.

claim: The ultimate consequences of disrupted chromocenter formation has never been addressed.
source: While multiple factors such as epigenetic modifications and transcription of repetitive DNA from pericentromeric DNA sequences are known to be required for chromocenter formation (Peters et al., 2001; Probst et al., 2010; Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012; Pinheiro et al., 2012; Hahn et al., 2013), the ultimate consequences of disrupted chromocenter formation has never been addressed, leaving the function of chromocenters unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The function of chromocenters is unknown.
source: While multiple factors such as epigenetic modifications and transcription of repetitive DNA from pericentromeric DNA sequences are known to be required for chromocenter formation (Peters et al., 2001; Probst et al., 2010; Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012; Pinheiro et al., 2012; Hahn et al., 2013), the ultimate consequences of disrupted chromocenter formation has never been addressed, leaving the function of chromocenters unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: D1 in Drosophila melanogaster contains 10 AT-hooks.
source: D1 in Drosophila melanogaster and HMGA1 in mouse are multi-AT-hook proteins; D1 contains 10 AT-hooks, HMGA1 contains three AT-hooks and both proteins contain C-terminal acidic domains (Aulner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior characterization of these proteins.

claim: HMGA1 in mouse contains three AT-hooks.
source: D1 in Drosophila melanogaster and HMGA1 in mouse are multi-AT-hook proteins; D1 contains 10 AT-hooks, HMGA1 contains three AT-hooks and both proteins contain C-terminal acidic domains (Aulner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior characterization of these proteins.

claim: Both D1 and HMGA1 contain C-terminal acidic domains.
source: D1 in Drosophila melanogaster and HMGA1 in mouse are multi-AT-hook proteins; D1 contains 10 AT-hooks, HMGA1 contains three AT-hooks and both proteins contain C-terminal acidic domains (Aulner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior characterization of these proteins.

claim: D1 is known to bind the Drosophila {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
source: D1 and HMGA1 are known to bind the Drosophila {AATAT}n satellite DNA (~8% of the Drosophila male diploid genome) and mouse major satellite DNA (~6% of the mouse genome), respectively (Goodwin et al., 1973; Rodriguez Alfageme et al., 1980; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982b; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982a; Lund et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies demonstrating this binding.

claim: {AATAT}n satellite DNA comprises approximately 8% of the Drosophila male diploid genome.
source: D1 and HMGA1 are known to bind the Drosophila {AATAT}n satellite DNA (~8% of the Drosophila male diploid genome) and mouse major satellite DNA (~6% of the mouse genome), respectively (Goodwin et al., 1973; Rodriguez Alfageme et al., 1980; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982b; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982a; Lund et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: HMGA1 is known to bind mouse major satellite DNA.
source: D1 and HMGA1 are known to bind the Drosophila {AATAT}n satellite DNA (~8% of the Drosophila male diploid genome) and mouse major satellite DNA (~6% of the mouse genome), respectively (Goodwin et al., 1973; Rodriguez Alfageme et al., 1980; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982b; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982a; Lund et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies demonstrating this binding.

claim: Mouse major satellite DNA comprises approximately 6% of the mouse genome.
source: D1 and HMGA1 are known to bind the Drosophila {AATAT}n satellite DNA (~8% of the Drosophila male diploid genome) and mouse major satellite DNA (~6% of the mouse genome), respectively (Goodwin et al., 1973; Rodriguez Alfageme et al., 1980; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982b; Levinger and Varshavsky, 1982a; Lund et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: The {AATAT}n satellite is distributed across 11 loci on multiple chromosomes.
source: The {AATAT}n satellite is distributed across 11 loci on multiple chromosomes as visualized by DNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on mitotic chromosome spreads (Figure 1B) (Lohe et al., 1993; Jagannathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: {AATAT}n satellite is typically clustered into a few foci in Drosophila interphase nuclei, colocalizing with the D1 protein.
source: However, it is typically clustered into a few foci in Drosophila interphase nuclei, colocalizing with the D1 protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The D1/{AATAT}n foci stained positively for H3K9me2 in interphase nuclei.
source: The D1/{AATAT}n foci stained positively for H3K9me2 in interphase nuclei (Figure 1C), a well-established characteristic of constitutive heterochromatin/chromocenters (Guenatri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: H3K9me2 is a well-established characteristic of constitutive heterochromatin/chromocenters.
source: The D1/{AATAT}n foci stained positively for H3K9me2 in interphase nuclei (Figure 1C), a well-established characteristic of constitutive heterochromatin/chromocenters (Guenatri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: D1 localized near the centromere (marked by Drosophila CENP-A, Cid) on mitotic chromosome spreads.
source: Consistently, D1 localized near the centromere (marked by Drosophila CENP-A, Cid) on mitotic chromosome spreads (marked by phospho-H3 S10) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: D1 is a chromocenter-localizing protein, via its binding to the {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
source: These results suggest that D1 is a chromocenter-localizing protein, via its binding to the {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data presented.

claim: The mouse HMGA1 protein was originally identified as an abundant non-histone component of mammalian chromatin.
source: The mouse HMGA1 protein was originally identified as an abundant non-histone component of mammalian chromatin (Goodwin et al., 1973; Lund et al., 1983) with subsequent studies demonstrating its binding to satellite DNA (Strauss and Varshavsky, 1984; Radic et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Subsequent studies demonstrated HMGA1 binding to satellite DNA.
source: The mouse HMGA1 protein was originally identified as an abundant non-histone component of mammalian chromatin (Goodwin et al., 1973; Lund et al., 1983) with subsequent studies demonstrating its binding to satellite DNA (Strauss and Varshavsky, 1984; Radic et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Mouse major satellite is present in pericentromeric regions of all chromosomes.
source: Mouse major satellite, which is present in pericentromeric regions of all chromosomes (Figure 1E) (Lyon and Searle, 1989), clustered into DAPI-dense chromocenters positive for HMGA1 protein (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is stated with a citation and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mouse major satellite clustered into DAPI-dense chromocenters positive for HMGA1 protein.
source: Mouse major satellite, which is present in pericentromeric regions of all chromosomes (Figure 1E) (Lyon and Searle, 1989), clustered into DAPI-dense chromocenters positive for HMGA1 protein (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Drosophila D1 protein localizes to major satellite/chromocenters when ectopically expressed in multiple mouse cell lines.
source: Interestingly, we found that Drosophila D1 protein localizes to major satellite/chromocenters when ectopically expressed in multiple mouse cell lines (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: D1 and HMGA1 may possess an orthologous and conserved function as satellite DNA/chromocenter-binding proteins.
source: Interestingly, we found that Drosophila D1 protein localizes to major satellite/chromocenters when ectopically expressed in multiple mouse cell lines (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that D1 and HMGA1 may possess an orthologous and conserved function as satellite DNA/chromocenter-binding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-species localization data.

claim: D1LL03310 and D1EY05004 are protein null alleles.
source: We used two D1 alleles, D1LL03310 and D1EY05004, which we show to be protein null alleles, evidenced by near-complete loss of anti-D1 antibody staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Combining D1LL03310 or D1EY05004 with the D1 deficiency allele Df(3R)BSC666 led to severe declustering of {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
source: When these alleles were combined with the D1 deficiency allele, Df(3R)BSC666, it led to severe declustering of {AATAT}n satellite DNA (Figure 1H–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1H–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: D1 is required for clustering of pericentromeric satellite DNA into chromocenters.
source: When these alleles were combined with the D1 deficiency allele, Df(3R)BSC666, it led to severe declustering of {AATAT}n satellite DNA (Figure 1H–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E), suggesting that D1 is required for clustering of pericentromeric satellite DNA into chromocenters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the declustering phenotype observed in D1 mutants.

claim: D1's requirement for chromocenter formation was observed in multiple cell types.
source: We observed D1's requirement for chromocenter formation in multiple cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–I), but we largely focused on spermatogonial cells, where the phenotypes (such as cell death) were most penetrant and severe.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–I.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of HMGA1 led to near complete loss of HMGA1 protein.
source: Following siRNA-mediated knockdown of HMGA1, which led to near complete loss of HMGA1 protein (see Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B,D–E for efficiencies of HMGA1 knockdown)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B,D–E.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of HMGA1 resulted in chromocenter disruption in multiple mouse cell lines.
source: Following siRNA-mediated knockdown of HMGA1, which led to near complete loss of HMGA1 protein (see Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B,D–E for efficiencies of HMGA1 knockdown), we observed chromocenter disruption in multiple mouse cell lines (Figure 1K–M, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J–L).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1K–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2J–L.

claim: D1 and HMGA1 have an orthologous function to organize pericentromeric satellite DNA into chromocenters.
source: These results suggest that D1 and HMGA1 have an orthologous function to organize pericentromeric satellite DNA into chromocenters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar chromocenter disruption phenotypes in both Drosophila and mouse systems.

claim: D1 mutation resulted in a significant increase in micronuclei formation.
source: We found that D1 mutation as well as siRNA-mediated HMGA1 knockdown in multiple mouse cell lines resulted in a significant increase in micronuclei formation (Figure 2A–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2A–F.

claim: siRNA-mediated HMGA1 knockdown in multiple mouse cell lines resulted in a significant increase in micronuclei formation.
source: We found that D1 mutation as well as siRNA-mediated HMGA1 knockdown in multiple mouse cell lines resulted in a significant increase in micronuclei formation (Figure 2A–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Micronuclei are known to have compromised nuclear envelope integrity.
source: Micronuclei are known to have compromised nuclear envelope integrity, leading to DNA damage and catastrophic chromosomal rearrangement therein (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Compromised nuclear envelope integrity in micronuclei leads to DNA damage and catastrophic chromosomal rearrangement.
source: Micronuclei are known to have compromised nuclear envelope integrity, leading to DNA damage and catastrophic chromosomal rearrangement therein (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Loss of D1 led to breaching of the nuclear envelope both in major and micronuclei.
source: We found that loss of D1 led to breaching of the nuclear envelope both in major and micronuclei, visualized by the cytoplasmic leakage of nuclear GFP (nlsGFP) (Figure 2G–I)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2G–I.

claim: Nuclear envelope integrity might be generally compromised in D1 mutant.
source: We found that loss of D1 led to breaching of the nuclear envelope both in major and micronuclei, visualized by the cytoplasmic leakage of nuclear GFP (nlsGFP) (Figure 2G–I), suggesting that nuclear envelope integrity might be generally compromised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nuclear envelope breaching observed in D1 mutants.

claim: Lamin surrounded the nucleus incompletely in D1 mutant spermatogonia (68.9% in D1 mutant vs. 1.9% in control).
source: We frequently observed that lamin surrounded the nucleus incompletely in D1 mutant (1.9% in control (n = 52) and 68.9% in D1 mutant (n = 58)) (Figure 2J,K, arrows indicate lamin-negative regions on the nuclear membrane).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Cytoplasmic 'holes' were observed in D1 mutant that resemble the nucleus in that they exclude cytoplasmic proteins such as Vasa, but are devoid of nuclear lamin.
source: We also observed cytoplasmic 'holes', which resemble the nucleus in that they exclude cytoplasmic proteins such as Vasa (Figure 2K, arrowhead), but are devoid of nuclear lamin (Figure 2K, arrowhead).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Cytoplasmic 'holes' in D1 mutant were often surrounded by an ER marker.
source: These 'holes' were often surrounded by an ER marker, which normally surrounds the nuclear envelope (Figure 2J) (Dorn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Otefin showed perturbed localization in D1 mutant (24.5% in D1 mutant vs. 2.7% in control).
source: Similarly, Otefin, an inner nuclear membrane LEM-domain protein (Barton et al., 2014), also showed perturbed localization (2.7% in control (n = 109) and 24.5% in D1 mutant (n = 106)) (Figure 2L,M, arrows indicate lamin/Otefin negative regions on the nuclear envelope while the arrowhead indicates Otefin-positive micronuclei).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 2L,M.

claim: D1 mutant cells exhibit compromised nuclear envelope integrity, which is associated with micronuclei formation.
source: Taken together, these results show that D1 mutant cells exhibit compromised nuclear envelope integrity, which is associated with micronuclei formation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the nuclear envelope and micronuclei data presented.

claim: Defects in nuclear envelope integrity can lead to extensive DNA damage in the major nucleus and micronuclei.
source: It has been shown that defects in nuclear envelope integrity can lead to extensive DNA damage in the major nucleus and micronuclei (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015; Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Nuclear envelope defects and extensive DNA damages therein lead to catastrophic chromosomal breaks/rearrangements termed chromothripsis.
source: Nuclear envelope defects and extensive DNA damages therein lead to catastrophic chromosomal breaks/rearrangements termed chromothripsis (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: Catastrophic DNA breaks/rearrangements are speculated to lead to tumorigenesis.
source: Such catastrophic DNA breaks/rearrangements are speculated to lead to tumorigenesis (Hatch and Hetzer, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior speculation.

claim: Extensive DNA damage (revealed by γ-H2Av) was observed in both major and micronuclei in D1 mutant.
source: Consistent with defective nuclear envelope integrity, we observed extensive DNA damage (revealed by γ-H2Av) in both major and micronuclei (Figure 3A–F, arrows point to damaged DNA in micronuclei in B and D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3A–F.

claim: D1 mutant testes rapidly degenerated.
source: Likely as a result of DNA damage and defective nuclear envelope integrity, D1 mutant testes rapidly degenerated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Knockdown of Omi in D1 mutant testes restored the cellularity.
source: When Omi, a gene required to promote germ cell death (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013), was knocked down in D1 mutant testes, it restored the cellularity in D1 mutant testis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: This is stated with a citation and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Surviving cells in D1 mutant testes with Omi knockdown showed a dramatic increase in DNA damage.
source: When Omi, a gene required to promote germ cell death (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013), was knocked down in D1 mutant testes, it restored the cellularity in D1 mutant testis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), but the surviving cells showed a dramatic increase in DNA damage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: Surviving germ cells in D1 mutant testes with Omi knockdown showed a high frequency of chromosome breaks compared to control (15.8% in D1 mutant vs. 3.7% in control).
source: Under these conditions, we observed that surviving germ cells in D1 mutant testes showed a high frequency of chromosome breaks compared to control, revealed by FISH on metaphase chromosome spreads from spermatocytes (3.7% in control (n = 27) vs. 15.8% in D1 mutant (n = 57)) (Figure 3G,H, arrowheads indicate sites of chromosome breaks).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Loss of D1/HMGA1 results in compromised nuclear envelope integrity, leading to extensive DNA damage and chromosomal breaks.
source: These results show that loss of D1/HMGA1 results in compromised nuclear envelope integrity, leading to extensive DNA damage and chromosomal breaks.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the DNA damage and chromosome break data presented.

claim: D1 mutation did not result in an increase in lagging chromosomes in spermatogonia.
source: However, we did not observe an increase in lagging chromosomes in D1 mutant spermatogonia or HMGA1-depleted mouse cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G.

claim: HMGA1 knockdown did not result in an increase in lagging chromosomes in mouse cells.
source: However, we did not observe an increase in lagging chromosomes in D1 mutant spermatogonia or HMGA1-depleted mouse cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G.

claim: Micronuclei formed by budding from the interphase nucleus both in Drosophila spermatogonia and mouse cells.
source: Instead, time-lapse live observation showed that micronuclei formed by budding from the interphase nucleus both in Drosophila spermatogonia and mouse cells (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Control Drosophila spermatogonial cells stably maintained nuclear contents for a prolonged time period (only 1 event of nuclear blebbing without concurrent micronuclei formation over 1552 min of live imaging).
source: Control cells stably maintained nuclear contents for a prolonged time period (only 1 event of nuclear blebbing without concurrent micronuclei formation (as detected by H2Av-RFP) over 1552 min of live imaging) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D1 mutant spermatogonial cells showed budding off of nuclear contents and micronuclei formation in interphase (15 nuclear breaches with eight micronuclei formed over 3427 min of live imaging with a total budding duration of 172 min).
source: In contrast, D1 mutant cells showed budding off of nuclear contents and micronuclei formation in interphase (15 nuclear breaches with eight micronuclei formed over 3427 min of live imaging with a total budding duration of 172 min) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HMGA1 knockdown in mouse cells resulted in micronuclei formation during interphase (three micronuclei formed by budding over 5962 min of live imaging with a total budding duration of 310 min).
source: Similarly, live imaging in mouse cells using the Hoechst DNA dye revealed that HMGA1 knockdown also resulted in micronuclei formation during interphase (siControl – no micronuclei formation over 253 min of live observation, siHMGA1 – three micronuclei formed by budding over 5962 min of live imaging with a total budding duration of 310 min) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated with quantification and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Micronuclei in D1 mutant/HMGA1-knockdown cells are generated during interphase, via budding from the nucleus.
source: These results show that micronuclei in D1 mutant/HMGA1-knockdown cells are generated during interphase, via budding from the nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the live imaging data.

claim: Previous in vitro experiments indicated that HMGA1 is capable of crosslinking multiple DNA strands with individual AT-hooks binding AT-rich DNA strands.
source: Previous in vitro experiments indicated that HMGA1 is capable of crosslinking multiple DNA strands with individual AT-hooks binding AT-rich DNA strands (Vogel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Overexpression of Drosophila D1 in mouse cells enhanced chromocenter formation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: When Drosophila D1 was expressed in mouse cells, it localized to the chromocenter as described above (Figure 1G), and its overexpression enhanced chromocenter formation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5A–C): the higher the amount of D1 that was expressed in mouse cells, the fewer chromocenters per cell was observed (i.e. more clustering).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: D1 is sufficient to bundle its binding target, tethering it to chromocenter.
source: These results suggest that D1 is sufficient to bundle its binding target, tethering it to chromocenter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dose-dependent chromocenter clustering data.

claim: Artificial tethering of D1 protein to euchromatic LacO repeat DNA sequences was sufficient to bring LacO repeats to the chromocenter.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that artificial tethering of D1 protein to euchromatic LacO repeat DNA sequences was sufficient to bring LacO repeats to the chromocenter.
evidence: This is stated and supported by the LacI-D1 fusion experiment data.

claim: In control spermatogonial cells expressing wild type D1, LacO repeats were observed far away from the {AATAT}n satellite foci/chromocenters.
source: In control spermatogonial cells expressing wild type D1, LacO repeats were observed far away from the {AATAT}n satellite foci/chromocenters (Figure 5E,G, arrow indicates site of LacO repeats in interphase nucleus).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5E,G.

claim: In cells expressing the LacI-D1 chimeric protein, LacO repeats were recruited close to {AATAT}n/chromocenters.
